## Hotspot inventory

Eight files trip `high_fan_in_fan_out`. Sorted against the reported cutoffs (fan-in p95 = 9 / p99 = 10; fan-out p95 = 6 / p99 = 11):

| File | fan-in | fan-out | vs. cutoff | Co-located findings |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `src/utils.ts` | **18** | 1 | **1.8× p99** — outlier | large_file 425L, 7× sync I/O |
| `src/index.ts` | 4 | **17** | **1.5× p99** — outlier | large_file 460L, 6 god functions |
| `src/esbuild/index.ts` | 1 | 11 | = p99 | `runEsbuild` 237L (4.0×), 38-prop option bag |
| `src/plugin.ts` | 10 | 3 | = p99 | `buildFinished` 103L |
| `src/log.ts` | 9 | 0 | = p95 | 2 unprefixed booleans |
| `test/utils.ts` | 9 | 0 | = p95 | 1 sync I/O |
| `src/rollup.ts` | 0 | 7 | just over p95 | `getRollupConfig` 122L, False Identity |
| `src/api-extractor.ts` | 1 | 6 | = p95 | `rollupDtsFiles` 85L |

Only **two** files are genuine outliers. The other six sit exactly *on* a percentile boundary — that's threshold noise, not a signal, and it's why the triage list below is short.

The framing that drives the order: **fan-in and fan-out are not the same problem.** High fan-in means other files' blast radius runs through you — fixing it reduces risk *across the codebase*. High fan-out means you're a dependency sink — fixing it reduces *your own* comprehension surface and ripples almost nowhere. The question asked for blast-radius reduction, so fan-in leads.

## Triage order

**1. `src/utils.ts` — do this first** (`crime_00039`, `crime_00044`, `crime_00010`)

Fan-in 18, nearly double the p99 cutoff of 10; 29 transitive importers. It is the single largest blast-radius amplifier in the repo. Critically, **fan-out is 1** — it depends on almost nothing, so splitting it is a pure leaf operation: move functions into responsibility-scoped modules, re-export from `utils.ts` during transition, update specifiers. No dependency rewiring, no cycle risk.

It also has **no `large_function` findings** despite being 425 lines. That means it's *wide, not deep* — a bag of unrelated helpers (`removeFiles`, `ensureTempDeclarationDir`, …), which is exactly the shape a file split fixes cleanly. And `test_gap` is 0 here, the best-covered file on the list. Highest payoff, lowest execution risk.

**2. `src/plugin.ts` — but write tests first** (`crime_00008`, `crime_00002`)

Fan-in 10, sitting on the p99 cutoff, 29 transitive importers. `buildFinished` is 103 lines (1.7× threshold) and flagged as a class method whose invariants are shared with siblings — it carries `agent_risk` 0.54, the highest of any `large_function` finding in the report despite only medium severity. That gap between severity and agent risk is the point: it's not the biggest function, it's the biggest function *behind the widest door*.

The right move here is **extraction, not splitting**. Pull helpers out of `buildFinished`; the surface those 10 importers see doesn't change at all, so the refactor's actual blast radius is zero. The blocker: `test_gap` is 0.75 — effectively unprotected. Add characterization tests before touching it.

**3. `src/esbuild/index.ts`** (`crime_00069`, `crime_00022`, `crime_00040`)

Fan-out 11, fan-in **1**. Restructuring it ripples to one file. `runEsbuild` is 237 lines (4.0× threshold) and reads **38 distinct properties** off a single `options` bag — the strongest single-signal evidence in the whole report that one function is doing many jobs. Cheap to fix, well-scoped, and it de-risks item 4.

**4. `src/index.ts` — the biggest job, deliberately last** (`crime_00070`, `crime_00068`, `crimes 00023–00025`)

Fan-out 17 (1.5× the p99 cutoff) but fan-in only **4**. This is the worst *local* mess in the repo — 460 lines holding `build` (293L, 4.9×), an anonymous 274L arrow, `mainTasks` (194L), `normalizeOptions` (96L), `startWatcher` (79L), `buildAll` (75L) — plus `build` is a False Identity (`crime_00034`: safe-sounding name, calls `createLogger` and `removeFiles`).

It ranks last **not** because it's healthy but because fixing it reduces nobody else's blast radius. It's where agents land to make changes, so it's the top *agent-safety* target — but it's the most work and the least leverage on the codebase graph. Do it incrementally, function by function.

## Leave alone

- **`src/log.ts`** — fan-in 9, fan-out 0, and 30 transitive importers, the highest ripple count in the report. And its *only* findings are two unprefixed booleans. A small, single-purpose module with a wide audience is a **correctly designed utility**, not a crime. The finding's own suggested action is `treat_as_load_bearing`, not `split`. Maximum ripple cost, zero defect payoff. Don't touch. (Rename `onlyImportant`/`silent` only if they're module-local; if exported, even that isn't worth 9 files of churn.)
- **`test/utils.ts`** — fan-in 9 from 9 test files. That's a healthy shared test helper. Refactoring churns the entire suite for zero production benefit.
- **`src/rollup.ts`** — real crimes (`getRollupConfig` 122L, option bag, `Date.now()`), but **fan-in 0**: fixing it reduces blast radius for exactly zero files. Defer until someone touches it. One exception worth doing now regardless — `crime_00009`, a function named `get*` that calls `setSilent` and `removeFiles`. A "get" that deletes files is precisely the trap an agent walks into. Rename it; it's a one-line change with no importers to update.
- **`src/api-extractor.ts`** — fan-out 6 is *exactly* the p95 cutoff, well under p99's 11, with fan-in 1. Boundary noise. Skip.
- **`src/cli-main.ts`** — `main` at 153L is high severity, but 2 transitive importers and no connectivity finding. Not a hotspot.
- **`docs/README.md`** — 679 lines and flagged "high", but it's markdown with blast radius 0. Not a refactor target in any structural sense.

## Two caveats on this data

**Churn is 0 on all 87 findings.** Normally the sharpest hotspot signal is fan-in × churn — load-bearing *and* actively changing. That axis is dark here (no git history in the fixture), so this ranking is purely structural. If real churn data existed and, say, `src/plugin.ts` turned out to be the most-edited file, it would jump ahead of `utils.ts`.

**Don't trust the green test suite as a refactor safety net.** `src/utils.ts` shows `test_gap` 0, which is why I put it first — but the report also carries 12 `weak_test_signal` findings with **zero** assert calls (`test/index.test.ts`, `test/graphql.test.ts`, `test/shims.test.ts`, …) and 14 more with only weak matchers. Those tests prove the code ran, not that behavior is preserved. Before step 1, strengthen assertions in whichever of those files actually exercise `utils.ts`, or the "well-covered" designation is doing no work for you.
